label: autosave-cadence-vanilla
_why: WHAT DOES AN AUTOSAVE COST? The savegame instrument (ROADMAP step 3.5) makes cadence a design knob, and cadence is paid for in GAME wall clock: the engine stalls to serialise 13-55 MB. That cost was ESTIMATED at 4-13% for quarterly from save size alone, and the estimate was wrong.
_why_the_obvious_measurement_CANNOT_sett: ⚠⚠ THE AUTOSAVE IS PERFECTLY CONFOUNDED WITH THE YEARLY PULSE (user, 2026-08-11). A yearly autosave fires on 1 JANUARY, which is also when `on_yearly_pulse` runs - so comparing tick windows that contain an autosave against those that do not is not measuring the autosave, it is measuring JANUARY. Worse, the observer polls every ~20 s and the game advances ~5.7 in-game days per second, so a window spans ~114 days: a month cannot be resolved even in principle, let alone a sub-second stall inside it. Run 1 of 20260811_094048 gives 5.68 +/- 0.13 in-game days/s in windows holding a 1 January against 5.76 +/- 0.10 elsewhere - a difference of 0.079 +/- 0.162, t ~ 0.5. Read correctly that is an UPPER BOUND on the yearly pulse AND the autosave TOGETHER, not an estimate of the autosave: January is not distinguishably slower than any other month, which points at both being close to free but sizes neither.
_arms: BOTH ARMS ARE {kind: control} - vanilla + telemetry, zero gameplay content. The ONLY difference between them is `autosave_interval`: yearly (~100 saves per century) against quarteryear (~400).
_identification: ⭐ THIS IS WHY THE DESIGN WORKS WHERE THE PASSIVE MEASUREMENT DOES NOT. Both arms play the same century, so both run the SAME ~100 yearly pulses; only the number of autosaves differs, by ~300. The yearly pulse therefore cancels, and (mean quarterly wall - mean yearly wall) / 300 is the cost of one autosave with no confound to argue about. It also needs no within-run timing at all - just total wall clock per run, which meta.json already records to a tenth of a second. That is the difference between a designed contrast and a natural experiment read off a log.
_order: Y-Q-Y-Q interleaved, not blocked, for the same reason the three-arm batch interleaved: the confound being measured is a few percent, so any drift in machine state over ~10 hours must fall on both arms equally rather than on whichever ran second.
_secondary_value: These four runs are also vanilla references in their own right. Together with the two vanilla runs of 20260811_094048 that gives n=6 vanilla campaigns on one build, four of them at the same yearly cadence the earlier vanilla sessions (20260805_234555, 20260806_110926) used - which is what the 'is vanilla still what it was' question wants.
_what_it_cannot_say: It measures the cost of WRITING autosaves at two cadences on a VANILLA economy. It does NOT measure it on the mod (bigger saves, more building records - direction known, size not). ⚠ And it does not separate the engine's serialisation stall from the CONCURRENT ARCHIVER's file copy, which runs in both arms and copies 4x as much in the quarterly one: what it isolates is the marginal cost of an autosave AS WE TAKE THEM, archiver included, which is the operationally useful quantity but not the engine's own. If the difference lands near zero, that pair is worth separating (a -NoSaveHarvest quarterly run) before concluding the engine writes for free. Nor does it say anything about a save's cost at a SPEED other than the observer's - the stall is absolute seconds, so it is a larger share of a slower tick.
_reading_it: wall-clock difference / 300 = seconds per autosave. For scale: at ~140 min per vanilla century, 1 s per save is +3.6% for quarterly and +0.9% for yearly; 0.4 s per save (the current point estimate, itself not distinguishable from zero) is +1.4% and +0.4%. If the two arms land within a couple of minutes of each other, the answer is that cadence is not a wall-clock decision at all and should be chosen purely on resolution and disk.
_cost: 4 runs x 100 in-game years on vanilla. Measured vanilla span ~2h20, so ~9.5 h plus whatever the quarterly arm's own tax turns out to be - which is the number under test. Harvest is NOT in the measured window: it runs after run_observer returns, so it cannot contaminate wall_seconds.
_disk: the quarterly runs stand at ~400 saves x ~40 MB = ~16 GB each until the between-run harvest drains them; the yearly ones at ~4 GB. Peak is one run at a time. The archiver stops itself below 8 GB free.
